newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran fights U.S. sanctions with oil deals.
newsitem.headline: Iran fights U.S. sanctions with oil deals.

text.p: Iran is near to striking oil and gas development contracts with European and other foreign firms prepared to invest in Iran despite the threat of U.S. sanctions, Iranian officials said on Saturday.

But the key to future outside investment in the offshore petroleum potential will be the outcome of European Union efforts to water down U.S. sanctions aimed at punishing non-U.S. companies that deal with Iran, industry sources attending an energy conference in Isfahan said.

Iran will soon make a decision on a $2 billion plus expansion of its mammoth South Pars gas field and has awarded a $140 million dollar contract to develop its Balal oilfield in the Gulf to a British engineering firm, sources at the Iranian Petroleum Ministry said.
"I am sure we will make an announcement (on South Pars) in one month," said Mohammad Nejadhosseinian, Deputy Minister for International Affairs at the Iranian Petroleum Ministry.

France's Total is in advanced negotiations with the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) to develop South Pars gas field, crucial to Iran's plans to become a major gas exporting power in the next decade by supplying Turkey, Pakistan, India and eventually Europe.
"We are discussing a part of South Pars development. What we would like to do is finalise it as soon as possible," said Christophe de Margerie, Total vice president.
Royal Dutch/Shell has also been in the running for South Pars, one of the world's single largest offshore gas fields which Iran shares with Arab Qatar.
"We are still very interested in South Pars," said Shell's exploration director A.J. Parsley.
The British engineering firm Pell Frischmann has been awarded a "buyback" contract to develop the 80 million barrels of oil locked in Balal to produce up to 40,000 bpd of crude, sources at NIOC said.
Financing of the project has still to be put in place, industrial sources in Isfahan, Iran's second major city, said.

South Pars and Balal would be vulnerable to be penalised under the Iran-Libya sanctions act which allows the U.S. president to penalise non-U.S. firms that invest $40 million or more a year in the two states' oil and gas sectors.
"We hope to see progress between the U.S. and the EU on the (sanctions) legislation. Without that we are hamstung," said one European company executive attending the meeting.

A spat with the EU following a German court decision on April 10 that implicated Iran's leadership in political assassinations in Europe has also dented prospects for other investments in the short term, a company source said.

"It is a difficult time right now with the EU problem, American sanctions and the May 23 (Iranian presidential) elections. Perhaps it is not a suitable time to make a serious economic decision," a company source said.

"Anything after Sirri is probably going to be very difficult," said another manager, referring to a deal between Total and NIOC in 1995 to develop Sirri A and E offshore gas fields where first output is expected in 1998.

Final contracts for South Pars and Balal together with continuing negotiations for the offshore Doroud and Salman Khuff fields would represent a major move forward in Iran's attempt to secure vital foreign investment in its oilfields.
Foreign investment in Iran's oil sector is seen as playing a key role in the country's attempt to maintain its role as the world's third largest oil exporter in the next decade.
This open-door petroleum policy was first shown in 1991 but relaunched in 1995 when NIOC offered 11 "buyback" projects worth some $6 billion to international and local firms.
